scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The farruca developed as a flamenco style in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
The word relates to 'farruco', an Andalusian term applied to immigrants from Galicia or Asturias, as well as a familiar nickname for Francisco.
While lyric references to Galician bagpipes and landscape led many to claim a northern origin, musicologists note this has not been scientifically proven.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Farruca carries an austere, dramatic, and sombre character linked symbolically to valor and restraint.
Unlike communal festive palos, it is primarily a theatrical and concert performance form.

Its dramatic gravity was spotlighted in major theatrical works, including Manuel de Falla's 1919 ballet El sombrero de tres picos (as the Miller's Dance / Danse du meunier) choreographed by Léonide Massine, and Carlos Saura's film Carmen featuring Antonio Gades.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The farruca is danced as a dramatic solo characterized by upright posture, sharp footwork (zapateado), held poses, sudden pauses, turns, and abrupt directional changes.
Performed within an eight-beat compás consisting of two 4/4 bars with accents on 1, 3, 5, and 7, it begins at a moderate, articulated tempo.
Choreographies proceed from an entrance (salida) into marked compás, llamadas, remates, and extended escobillas.
Watch for Llamada, Escobilla, Remate.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (3j5IRvgQAS8)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo stage performance utilizing abrupt changes of direction and level.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Farruca music is grounded in binary or quadruple meter (two measures of 4/4) with strong accents on counts 1, 3, 5, and 7.
The primary accompanying instrument is the flamenco guitar, traditionally played in A minor or E minor, characterized by alternation between E7 and A minor, rasgueados, falsetas, and golpes.
Listen for the Flamenco guitar, Palmas, Voice.
The pulse is 4/4 (two measures of 4/4 forming an 8-count compás).

A serious minor-key flamenco guitar structure driven by alternating E7 and A minor chords. Sharp rasgueados and percussive strikes punctuate sustained melodic falsetas, characterized by dramatic silences that resolve into rapid acoustic footwork.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance emerged within theatrical spaces, varieté, and cafés cantantes before transitioning to concert halls and ballet stages.
Performers wear attire that accentuates vertical line and sharp posture, traditionally consisting of high-waisted trousers, fitted waistcoats, and flamenco boots suitable for virtuosic footwork.
Historical descriptions document the use of a cape during early male stage performances.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dancer Faíco (Francisco Mendoza Ríos) and guitarist Ramón Montoya are recognized as the primary architects of the modern dance and guitar structure.
Dancers El Gato, Antonio de Bilbao, Manolito la Rosa, El Batato, Antonio Gades, El Güito, Mario Maya, and Manolete further codified its stage aesthetic.
Farruca belongs to the aflamencado group of non-Andalusian folkloric forms along with the garrotín.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Farruca is sibling of Garrotín: Both are early twentieth-century aflamencado palos derived from non-Andalusian folkloric roots and shaped by Faíco.
Farruca is parent of Tangos: Shares the foundational binary compás structure, though farruca adopts a minor key and dramatic, sober mood.
Farruca is sibling of Tientos: Shares the measured four-beat rhythmic framework and gravity of expression.
Farruca is influence of Tanguillo: Shares tempo characteristics and sometimes provides rhythmic material for the farruca's closing stretta.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
